page: Amazon Web Services r8a.2xlarge is a memory-optimized instance built on the Nitro system, powered by an AMD EPYC 9R45 processor based on the x86_64 architecture. The instance provides 8 dedicated physical cores running at clock speeds up to 4.5 GHz with a single thread per core, avoiding hardware multithreading contention. It includes 64.0 GB of high-speed DDR5 memory operating at 6 GHz, establishing an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU allocation. The CPU features 48 KB of L1 data cache, 1.0 MB of L2 cache, 32 MB of shared L3 cache, and support for vector extensions including AVX-512, VNNI, and BF16. Baseline network throughput is configured at 4 Gbps, while local instance storage is not included, requiring external block storage for persistent data.

Benchmark evaluations demonstrate strong single-thread execution characteristics alongside balanced multi-core throughput. The instance achieves top-tier results in stress-ng single-core tests, single-threaded gzip compression, single-threaded bzip3 decompression, and Geekbench single-core metrics. Text processing and small-scale language model text generation also score within the upper performance tiers. Conversely, multi-threaded tasks, including multi-core Geekbench, PassMark compute runs, and Clang compilation tests, align with the median distribution typical of an 8-core allocation. Memory throughput tests reveal uncached transfer rates of 54.65 GB/sec for reads and 34.27 GB/sec for writes.

The r8a.2xlarge balances resource density and per-core execution speed, making it suitable for memory-intensive services that do not require massive thread parallelization. The 1:8 core-to-memory ratio directly supports in-memory data structures, medium-scale Redis caches, operational relational databases, and memory-bound ETL transformations. The absence of integrated local storage means storage-heavy workloads must account for network-attached storage throughput overhead. Organizations running latency-sensitive memory tasks benefit from dedicated physical cores and top-tier single-core performance without investing in larger multi-socket instance tiers.
